summary.en: The United States signed a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela's interim government, and a U.S. marine died after falling overboard during a Caribbean operation linked to the renewed ties. Former oil minister Machado called for a more drastic overhaul of the oil sector amid hyperinflation, food shortages, massive emigration and socioeconomic collapse. Venezuelan grassroots groups rejected the agreement and denounced what they called a normalization of subordination, while military prisoners entered a third week without food and families took the fight to court. Two battle-related deaths were recorded in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: USA signerte en militær samarbeidsavtale med Venezuelas midlertidige regjering, og en amerikansk marine døde etter å ha falt overbord under en karibisk operasjon knyttet til de fornyede båndene. Den tidligere oljeministeren Machado oppfordret til en mer drastisk omlegging av oljesektoren midt i hyperinflasjon, matmangel, massiv emigrasjon og sosialøkonomisk kollaps. Venezuelas grasrotgrupper avviste avtalen og fordømte det de kalte en normalisering av underordning, mens militærfanger gikk inn i en tredje uke uten mat og familier tok kampen til retten. To kamprelaterte dødsfall ble registrert i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro as well as Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
